summary:
Has Bean Planned helps rice farmers decide what to do with their field in the dry season. A farmer answers five questions on a phone, in English or Filipino, and gets one plain answer: the best fit among leaving the field idle, mungbean, corn and peanut, with three reasons and traffic lights for water, soil, income and work. A second view gives cooperatives and extension workers the full comparison, a season calendar of bare field and vulnerable months, 24 past dry seasons replayed, and a shared planner.

It addresses the challenge by turning NASA data into a rotation choice a farmer can act on. GPM IMERG supplies rainfall, NASA POWER supplies temperature and soil wetness, and MODIS NDVI shows observed greenness. FAO crop-water methods convert these into water need, yield loss and income, and 300 what-if runs show how sure the answer is.

It matters because this one choice decides a smallholder's dry-season income. A crop that fails in an El Niño year costs the farmer the seed, labor and inputs already paid for; an idle field earns nothing and leaves the soil bare. Seeing the odds first helps a farmer avoid that loss. San Mateo, Isabela is our test-drive area; the design is meant to scale nationally. The tool supports, not replaces, farmer and expert judgement. Past seasons are not forecasts, simply a reference point.
details:
WHAT IT DOES:

Has Bean Planned compares four dry-season options after rice: leaving the field fallow, mungbean, yellow corn and peanut. It has two views that share every setting.

Farmer view: One question per screen, answered by tapping large picture cards: when the last rice was harvested, whether the field can be watered, sticky clay or loose soil, what matters most (up to two of safe harvest, healthy soil, more income, less work, animal feed), and whether a dry El Niño year is expected. The farmer then sees one answer card with three plain reasons, a fit score, four traffic lights that use marks and words as well as color, how sure the answer is, what a dry year would change, and a "what if it rains less?" slider.

Analytics and Community view: Five tabs for extension workers and cooperatives: Compare (priority sliders, scenarios, ranked options with why-cards, editable prices and costs), Season calendar (bare-field periods and month-by-month water and heat flags), Past seasons (rainfall and heat trends, a replay of all 24 dry seasons, IMERG against POWER rainfall, MODIS NDVI), Plan together (seed, labor and water needs for a cooperative), and Data & methods (sources, a grid-cell map, every parameter with its status, a glossary and the limitations).

HOW IT WORKS

1. Rainfall from GPM IMERG and temperatures from NASA POWER are processed into 24 dry seasons (December to May, 2001-02 to 2024-25), each labelled El Niño, La Niña or neutral using NOAA's Oceanic Niño Index.

2. Crop water need is estimated from temperature (Hargreaves-Samani) and FAO-56 crop coefficients.

3. Water supply is usable rain plus water stored in the soil at planting.

4. The shortfall becomes yield loss through FAO-33 yield-response factors, then income from yield, price and cost.

5. Each option is scored on six criteria weighted by the farmer's priorities.

6. The comparison is re-run 300 times with inputs varied inside stated ranges, and every past season is replayed.

WHAT IT FOUND FOR SAN MATEO

Mungbean is the best fit in both a typical year and a strong El Niño year. In a strong El Niño year corn falls below leaving the field idle. Mungbean met at least 80% of its water need in all 24 past dry seasons.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

For the farmer, the dry-season choice is a bet made with money already spent. Seed, fertilizer and labor are paid for at planting, and if the rain does not come that money is gone. In our model, corn's return per hectare in a strong El Niño year falls to roughly an eighth of its return in a typical year, while mungbean's holds. Has Bean Planned lets a farmer see that difference before planting, not after harvest. It also shows the cost of doing nothing: an idle field earns no income for half the year and leaves the soil bare, while a legume such as mungbean adds nitrogen for the next rice crop.

A farmer who is not comfortable with technology can get a grounded answer in about a minute, and see why. Cooperatives and agriculture offices can plan seed, labor and water together and see which months are most exposed. Every number is traceable and labelled Sourced, Local source, Secondary source, Assumption or Illustrative, so users know what to trust and what to replace with their own figures.

SCALING

San Mateo, Isabela is our test-drive area. Every data source is global and fetched by coordinates, so the next steps are a location picker, regional prices, more crops and more Philippine languages.

TOOLS

JavaScript with React 18, Vite and Tailwind CSS; Recharts for charts; Leaflet with OpenStreetMap for the map; Python (pandas, NumPy, requests) for the data pipeline; Vitest and pytest for 41 automated tests; GitHub and Netlify for hosting. SI tools (Claude and Claude Code by Anthropic, and Gemini for an early literature summary) were used for coding, drafting and source checking; this is disclosed in SI_DISCLOSURE.md in the repository.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

The same model serves two audiences: a picture card flow that gives one answer, and a full analyst view. We chose transparent rules over a black-box model so a farmer or extension worker can check the reasoning. The app states its own uncertainty and shows a "close call" note when the answer is not clear cut.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Scenarios summarize past seasons and are not forecasts; satellite and model grids are not rain gauges; one point is modelled; there is no pest model and no field validation yet. Crop prices are Philippine Statistics Authority farmgate prices for Cagayan Valley (January to May 2026), and mungbean and peanut production costs are PSA national averages for 2021; corn yield and cost and peanut yield are still placeholders, badged as such and editable. Accessibility and Readability: 18 px text, large touch targets, a 360 px layout, no meaning carried by color alone, and motion switched off on request.

Live app: https://hasbeanplanned.netlify.app
